title: Government by Lottery
description: Athens's jury machine, Venice's ten-round election of its doge, and citizens' assemblies today

concepts.title: The Machine That Picked Juries
concepts.contentHtml:
Ask most people what makes a government democratic and they will say elections. An Athenian of the fourth century BC might have said the opposite. Most of the city's officials were not elected at all: they were picked by lot from the citizens who put their names forward.1 The generals were the main exception. War was too dangerous to leave to chance, so the assembly chose them by show of hands.2

Aristotle stated the principle plainly. Filling offices by lot was thought to be democratic, and filling them by election oligarchic.3 Elections favor the famous, the rich and the persuasive. A lottery gives every citizen in the pool the same chance.

For the courts, where hundreds of jurors could sit on a single case, Athens built a machine. The kleroterion was a stone slab cut with rows of slots, and each juror's ticket, carrying his name, his father's name and his district, went into a slot.4 Bronze tickets of this kind have been found, and fragments of the slabs survive in the Agora museum in Athens.5 An official dropped black and white bronze dice down a tube on the side, and each one settled a whole row of tickets at once.6 Nobody could know in advance who would judge a case, which made bribing a jury very hard.

concepts.title: Ten Rounds to Elect a Doge
concepts.contentHtml:
Venice took the lottery further than anyone. Its head of state, the doge, ruled for life, and the great families feared nothing more than a rival capturing the office. So from 1268 the doge was chosen in ten rounds. The Great Council, then about 480 men,1 drew 30 of its members by lot. A second lot cut them to 9, and the 9 named a college of 40, each name needing 7 of their 9 votes.2 A lot cut the 40 to 12, who named 25; a lot cut those to 9, who named 45; a lot cut those to 11, who named 41. The 41 elected the doge, who needed at least 25 of their votes. The same machine ran until the Republic fell in 1797.

At first an official drew the lots. From 1328 the job went to a boy: on election day the youngest member of the inner council prayed in St Mark's Basilica, and the first boy he saw on leaving became the ballottino, who pulled the balls from the urn.3 English still carries a trace of it. Ballot comes from the Venetian ballotta,4 a small ball used to register a vote.5

The design does two things. Until the last draw, nobody knows who the electors will be, so there is no one to bribe or threaten ahead of time. And every name needs a supermajority, so a faction with a bare majority cannot simply install its own people; it needs luck in the draws, or allies. The Great Council grew to more than two thousand members,6 and the machine kept working. The Doge Machine lab runs it: in its simple model, even a faction holding 60% of the council gets its own doge only about six times in ten.

concepts.title: Lotteries Today
concepts.contentHtml:
The lottery never quite left politics. Juries in many countries are still drawn at random from the voters' roll. And since the 2010s several governments have tried citizens' assemblies: a random sample of ordinary people, balanced by age, sex and region, who hear from experts and campaigners over several weekends and then make recommendations.

Ireland has used them most. Its Convention on the Constitution mixed 66 randomly chosen citizens with 33 politicians and an independent chair.1 One of its recommendations, to allow same-sex marriage, went to a referendum in 2015, which passed with 62.1% of the vote.2 The Citizens' Assembly that followed had 99 citizen members and a chair appointed by the government.3 In 2017 it voted 51 to 38 that the constitution's Eighth Amendment, which banned abortion in almost all cases, should be replaced by a provision letting parliament legislate.4 In May 2018 voters agreed, by 66.4% to 33.6%.5

The case for choosing by lot is the Athenian one: a random sample looks like the public, owes nothing to donors and never has to win the next election. The case against is that a lottery gives power to people nobody chose and nobody can vote out. So far the assemblies have advised rather than decided, and elected politicians or the voters themselves have kept the final word.

title: Voting Someone Out
description: Ostracism, a well full of pre-written ballots, and stranger ways to remove a ruler

concepts.title: Ostracism
concepts.contentHtml:
Athens had a way to vote a politician out of the city. Each year the assembly voted on whether to hold an ostracism.1 If it said yes, citizens later gathered and each scratched a name on an ostrakon, a broken piece of pottery. If fewer than six thousand voted, the ostracism was void.2 (One ancient tradition says instead that six thousand had to vote against the same man.3) The man named most often had to leave Athens for ten years, but he kept the income from his property.4 The first person banished this way was Hipparchus son of Charmus, in 487 BC.5

Ostracism needed no crime. It was a vote against a person: a way to remove someone who looked too powerful before he could make himself a tyrant, or to settle a feud between two leaders by sending one away. Plutarch tells of an illiterate voter who handed his shard to a stranger and asked him to write "Aristides" on it.6 The stranger asked what Aristides had done to him. Nothing, said the man; he was just tired of hearing him called "the Just." The stranger was Aristides himself, and he wrote his own name. He was ostracized soon after, around 482 BC.7

The device ended in farce. Around 416 BC the two leading men of Athens, Nicias and Alcibiades, each looked likely to be ostracized. They pooled their supporters, and the vote fell on Hyperbolus instead,8 a lesser politician whom neither had meant to exile.9 He was the last man ever ostracized.10 The annual vote stayed on the calendar, but Athens never used it again.

concepts.title: The Stuffed Ballots of Themistocles
concepts.contentHtml:
Thousands of ostraka survive, because once a shard was counted it was rubbish, and rubbish went into wells and pits. The names on them read like a roll call of early Athenian democracy, and one of the most common is Themistocles, the general who built the navy that beat the Persians at Salamis.

In 1937 the archaeologist Oscar Broneer was excavating a well on the north slope of the Acropolis. Among the objects in it were 191 ostraka, and all but one bore the name of Themistocles.1 When Broneer studied the handwriting, he found that just fourteen people had written them all, which showed beyond doubt that they were not inscribed by the voters themselves.2

Nobody writes 190 ballots for their own use. Broneer concluded that Themistocles' opponents had prepared the shards in bulk, on matching pottery, to hand out to citizens on the day,3 perhaps to voters who could not write. These ones were never cast; they ended up at the bottom of the well. But they show that the most direct democracy in history already had campaign organizers, mass-produced ballots and votes written by someone other than the voter.

concepts.title: Shooting Stars and Clan Mothers
concepts.contentHtml:
Other peoples built their own ways to remove a ruler. Sparta had two kings at once, and five officials called ephors, elected each year, to watch them. According to Plutarch, every ninth year the ephors chose a clear, moonless night and sat in silence watching the sky.1 If a star shot across it, they took it as a sign that the kings had offended the gods, and suspended them until an oracle from Delphi or Olympia came to their rescue. Around 242 BC an ephor named Lysander announced that he had seen the sign and brought charges against King Leonidas II, who was deposed.2

Among the Haudenosaunee, the Iroquois Confederacy, each chief, called Hoyaneh, is chosen by the Clan Mother of his clan.3 The same woman can remove him. If he fails to represent the clan, she warns him, and if he still fails she can take away his position;4 removing chiefs is left to her authority.5 The act is known as dehorning, after the antlers that mark a chief's office.

Modern democracies mostly remove leaders by beating them at the next election, or by impeachment for misconduct. Some US states also allow a recall, in which a petition forces a special vote on whether an official should stay in office before the term is up. It is the nearest thing today to an ostracism: no crime required, only enough people who want someone gone.

title: Ties and Dead Winners
description: Elections settled from a bowl, won by the dead, or too close to call

concepts.title: Decided by Lot
concepts.contentHtml:
Elections end in exact ties more often than you might think, especially small ones, and most US states have a rule ready. A 2014 survey by the Washington Post found that 35 states settled a tie with a coin toss, a drawing or some other game of chance.1 Virginia's law says that when the candidates tie, the State Board of Elections shall publicly determine by lot which of them is elected.2

In 2017 that law decided who ran Virginia's House of Delegates. In the 94th District, a December recount put the Democrat, Shelly Simonds, ahead of the Republican, David Yancey, by a single vote.3 Then a three-judge court counted one disputed ballot for Yancey, and certified the race as tied at 11,608 votes each.4 On January 4, 2018, the board put each name in a film canister, put the canisters in a bowl, and drew one.5 It was Yancey's, and with that seat Republicans held the House 51 to 49.6

A lot does not always settle things. In Mississippi in 2015 a state House race tied at 4,589 votes each, and the candidates drew straws.7 The winner of the draw was later unseated when the state House reviewed the ballots and seated his opponent instead.8 Elsewhere, a tied 2011 primary in North Las Vegas was settled by drawing cards (a king of diamonds beat a five),9 and in 2019 a Philippine town got its mayor by a best-of-three coin toss.10

concepts.title: Elected After Death
concepts.contentHtml:
Ballots are printed weeks before an election, and the law often forbids changing them late. So candidates who die during the campaign sometimes win anyway.

On October 16, 1972, a small plane carrying House Majority Leader Hale Boggs of Louisiana and Representative Nick Begich of Alaska disappeared on a campaign flight from Anchorage to Juneau.1 It was never found. That November both men were re-elected, although they had not been found.2

In 2000 the governor of Missouri, Mel Carnahan, was running for the US Senate when he was killed in a plane crash three weeks before election day. His name stayed on the ballot, because state law prohibited changes within a month of the election.3 On November 7 he beat the sitting senator, John Ashcroft. The new governor, Roger Wilson, offered the seat to Carnahan's widow, Jean,4 who was appointed to fill the vacancy caused by her husband's death.5 And in 2018 a Nevada brothel owner and reality TV figure, Dennis Hof, was found dead on October 16;6 it was too late to take his name off the ballots, which had already been printed and mailed,7 and he won his seat in the state Assembly anyway.

concepts.title: Too Close to Call
concepts.contentHtml:
The closest election in the history of the US Senate took ten months to decide.1 In November 1974, Louis Wyman, a Republican, and John Durkin, a Democrat, ran for an open seat in New Hampshire. On election day Wyman won by just 355 votes.2 A recount gave the seat to Durkin by 10. The state's ballot commission then looked again and gave it to Wyman by 2.

The Constitution makes each chamber the judge of its own members' elections, so the dispute went to the Senate. Senators spent months arguing over disputed ballots without agreeing. In the end the Senate declared the seat vacant, and a former senator, Norris Cotton, held it until a new election on September 16, 1975.3 Turnout broke records, and Durkin won the rerun by about 27,000 votes.4

Ties and razor-thin results expose something elections usually hide. Every count has an error rate: a few ballots misread, misplaced or disputed. When the margin is smaller than the error, the count cannot say who really won, and the result rests on a rule chosen in advance: a recount, a rerun, a court or a lot.

title: Accidents of the Rulebook
description: A filibuster nobody planned, an amendment rescued by a term paper, and the tie that changed the Constitution

concepts.title: The Filibuster Nobody Planned
concepts.contentHtml:
The US Senate's most famous habit may have begun as housekeeping. Early on, the Senate's rules included a motion called the "previous question," which other assemblies use to bring a debate to an end. In 1805 Vice President Aaron Burr, presiding over the Senate in his last days in office, recommended that the chamber get rid of it.1 When senators met in 1806, they dropped the motion from the rule book.2

Political scientist Sarah Binder argues that this was a mistake nobody noticed for decades: with the motion gone, the Senate had no way to force a vote while anyone still wanted to talk. It took several decades for a minority to exploit the gap, leading to the first real filibuster in 1837.3 In 1841 a minority tried to run out the clock on a bill to create a national bank.4 Other historians doubt the old motion was ever used to cut off debate, so whether the change mattered as much as Binder thinks is still argued.

A cure came slowly. In 1917, at President Woodrow Wilson's urging, the Senate adopted Rule 22, which let it end debate by a two-thirds vote, a step called cloture.5 In 1975 it lowered the bar to three-fifths of the whole Senate, which is 60 of the 100 senators.6 That number, and not a simple majority, is why so many bills now need 60 votes to pass.

concepts.title: The C-Grade Amendment
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1789 James Madison proposed a set of constitutional amendments, and most of them became the Bill of Rights.1 One that did not would have stopped members of Congress from raising their own pay before the next election. Too few states ratified it, and it was forgotten.

In 1982 Gregory Watson, a 19-year-old sophomore, was taking a government class at the University of Texas at Austin.2 He wrote his paper on the forgotten amendment, arguing that because Congress had set no deadline it was technically still alive. He turned it in to the teaching assistant and got it back with a C.3 So he set out to prove it, writing letters to state legislators across the country, and one state after another ratified it. On May 7, 1992, Michigan provided what was thought to be the 38th ratification,4 the one that completed three-fourths of the states, and the amendment became the 27th. It had been proposed on September 25, 1789: 202 years earlier.5

Watson's grade stood for 35 years. In 2017 a University of Texas professor, Zach Elkins, arranged for it to be changed,6 and the original professor signed the form. It is now an A.

concepts.title: The Tie That Rewrote the Constitution
concepts.contentHtml:
The original Constitution gave each presidential elector two votes and did not let him say which was for president. The candidate with the most votes became president, and the runner-up vice president. In 1800 that design broke. Thomas Jefferson and his own running mate, Aaron Burr, each received 73 electoral votes.1 A tie went to the House of Representatives, where Jefferson's opponents were tempted to back Burr. On February 17, 1801, after 36 ballots, the House finally chose Jefferson.2

The fix was the 12th Amendment, ratified in 1804,3 which gave electors separate votes for president and vice president.4 Every presidential election since has run on it.

Amendments without a deadline can linger. Four proposed long ago, two in 1789, one in 1810 and one in 1861, are still technically pending before the states;5 one of the 1789 pair was the pay amendment that Watson revived. Only from the 18th Amendment onward did Congress make a habit of giving the states seven years to ratify.6 The 1861 proposal, the Corwin Amendment, would have shielded slavery from federal interference. It is the only proposed amendment ever signed by a president.7
